continuity: Robert E. Howard, “The Tower of the Elephant” (Weird Tales, March 1933)
work_or_witness: “The Tower of the Elephant,” chapters I–III
description: A Cimmerian thief who attempts to steal the Elephant's Heart from Yara's tower, joins Taurus for the ascent, survives the tower's defenses, and carries out Yag-kosha's requested act of release and vengeance.

cultures.note: Howard's fictional people/identity term in this story; no real-world equivalence is asserted.

roles_and_vocations.note: Conan identifies himself this way to Yag-kosha in chapter III; it is not an RPG class mapping.

artifacts_and_vehicles.note: Artifact attached as a dimension, never a node.

metaphysical_laws_and_rituals.note: The named final sorcery is Yag-kosha's account and instruction.

canon_status: named protagonist in the declared Howard story witness

citations.locator: Chapter I, paragraphs beginning “You spoke of the Elephant Tower” through the garden entry; Chapter II; Chapter III, lines 269–333
supports: Conan's Cimmerian identity, theft objective, partnership with Taurus, encounters, aid to Yag-kosha, and exit from the tower.

comparison_cautions: This is only the young Conan of one Howard story, not a composite franchise character.
Cimmerian and the story's depictions of people are fictional 1933 pulp vocabulary and must not be mapped onto real ethnic, national, or racial categories.

continuity: Robert E. Howard, “The Tower of the Elephant” (Weird Tales, March 1933)
work_or_witness: “The Tower of the Elephant,” chapter II
description: A Nemedian master thief who has planned the tower robbery, kills a guard, uses black-lotus powder to clear the garden, and dies in the tower's upper chamber.

cultures.note: Howard's fictional regional identity; no real-world equivalent is asserted.

artifacts_and_vehicles.note: A story artifact/tool, not an entity node.

canon_status: named material companion in the declared Howard story witness

citations.locator: Chapter II, paragraphs beginning “Taurus of Nemedia,” “By Bel, god of thieves,” “It was made from the black lotus,” and “The Nemedian stared up”
supports: Taurus's name, identity, theft plan, use of black-lotus powder, companionship with Conan, and death in the tower.

comparison_cautions: ‘Prince of thieves’ is a story epithet, not inherited royalty or a generic criminal-guild rank.
Nemedian is a fictional Howard term and is not mapped to real regional identity.

continuity: Robert E. Howard, “The Tower of the Elephant” (Weird Tales, March 1933)
work_or_witness: “The Tower of the Elephant,” chapters I and III
description: The tower's priest and sorcerer, identified as keeper of the Elephant's Heart. In Yag-kosha's testimony, Yara once learned from him, then enslaved and tortured him; Yara is destroyed by the story's final jewel-working.

roles_and_vocations.note: Titles used by the story; no universal religious or magic-class equivalence is claimed.

power_traditions.note: Story-specific power practice, not a standardized system.

states_and_transformations.term: shrinking and absorption into the jewel
states_and_transformations.note: Final story event; no generic transformation mapping.

artifacts_and_vehicles.note: Artifact associated with Yara's power in the story.

canon_status: named antagonist in the declared Howard story witness

citations.locator: Chapter I, paragraphs beginning “Why, any fool knows that Yara” and “Yara came not often”; Chapter III, paragraphs beginning “First he sat at my feet” through the tower's destruction
supports: Yara's tower and jewel, titles, alleged enslavement of Yag-kosha, confrontation with Conan, and final fate.

comparison_cautions: Yag-kosha's account of Yara's earlier acts is in-story testimony, though the final confrontation is directly narrated.
The story's period portrayal of exoticized places and peoples is not used as historical description.

continuity: Robert E. Howard, “The Tower of the Elephant” (Weird Tales, March 1933)
work_or_witness: “The Tower of the Elephant,” chapter III
description: The blinded captive in Yara's tower, named Yag-kosha and Yogah, who recounts an origin on Yag, asks Conan to perform the Blood-and-Jewel working, and becomes the green winged avenger seen in the jewel's final vision.

being_types.term: being of Yag, in Yag-kosha's own account
being_types.note: Self-reported origin and ontology; not classified as a real or generic alien, god, or demon type.

roles_and_vocations.term: former teacher of Yara, in Yag-kosha's account
roles_and_vocations.note: The prior teacher relationship is his testimony.

power_traditions.note: Yag-kosha specifies and initiates the story's named sorcery.

states_and_transformations.term: release from captive body / green winged form in the jewel vision
states_and_transformations.note: Directly narrated as Conan's final perception but not normalized as a generic afterlife state.

artifacts_and_vehicles.note: The jewel receives the blood and manifests the final event.

cosmologies_and_realms.note: Claimed home world, not independently validated beyond this tale.

canon_status: named material supernatural agent in the declared Howard story witness

citations.locator: Chapter III, paragraphs beginning “Who is here?”, “Oh man, listen”, “I am very old”, “First he sat at my feet”, and “Now for the great magic” through the final vision
supports: Yag-kosha/Yogah's names, captivity, self-account, relationship with Yara, requested ritual, and final appearance in the jewel vision.

comparison_cautions: Yag-kosha and Yogah are aliases for one individual, not separate nodes.
The tale's language about peoples and evolution is period pulp fiction and is neither endorsed nor treated as real anthropology.
